summary: Defines an experimental new DNS record type that lets the Domain Name System carry location information about hosts, networks and subnets.

eli5.summary: A new kind of entry in the Internet's phone book saying where on Earth a computer is.

questions: what is the dns loc record
how to put location info in dns
how does dns store location data
subtitle: Putting location coordinates into the Domain Name System

tldr.problem: The DNS can store IP addresses and mail servers, but not geographic location information. Network administrators need a way to associate physical locations with hosts and networks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1876 defines a new DNS record type called LOC that stores latitude, longitude, altitude and precision information as a 16-byte resource record.
tldr.outcome: The LOC record became an experimental mechanism for location-aware applications like network maps and traceroute visualizations, though it saw limited adoption.

today: RFC 1876 is an Experimental RFC from January 1996 and remains classified as Experimental. It has not been obsoleted, and the LOC record is registered in the DNS. However, adoption has been minimal; most location-based services use separate geographic databases or GPS services rather than DNS LOC records.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Location (LOC) record is a new DNS resource record type that allows the Domain Name System to store geographic location information about hosts, networks and subnets. Instead of looking up a location in a flat file or separate database, administrators can store latitude, longitude, altitude and accuracy estimates directly in the DNS.

The RFC was created as an experimental mechanism to test whether the DNS could serve as a carrier for location information, similar to how it replaced the HOSTS.TXT file for storing address information. It reserves DNS type code 29 and the mnemonic LOC for this purpose.
sections.eli5: DNS is like the Internet's phone book. This note adds a new entry type that says 'this computer is located here on Earth' instead of just 'this computer's address is such and such'.

sections.title: LOC Record Data Format
sections.content:
A LOC record is 16 octets (bytes) of binary data containing seven fields. The Version field must be zero. The Size field encodes the diameter of a sphere around the location as a base-10 exponent, allowing sizes from under 1 cm to 90,000 km. The Horizontal Precision and Vertical Precision fields describe accuracy in centimeters using the same encoding.

The Latitude, Longitude, and Altitude fields each occupy 32 bits. Latitude and longitude are expressed in thousandths of a second of arc, with 2^31 representing the equator and prime meridian respectively. Altitude is measured in centimeters relative to the WGS 84 ellipsoid used by GPS, with an offset of 100,000 meters.
sections.eli5: The data is like a shipping label: where it is (latitude and longitude), how high it is, and how big the area is. All written in a compact number format the computer understands.

sections.title: Master File Format and Examples
sections.content:
LOC records are written in DNS zone files in a human-readable format that looks like: example.com. LOC 42 21 54 N 71 06 18 W -24m, followed by optional size and precision values. The format uses degrees, minutes and seconds of latitude (0-90) and longitude (0-180), with N/S and E/W directions. If minutes and seconds are omitted they default to zero. Size defaults to 1 meter, horizontal precision to 10,000 meters (useful for postal codes), and vertical precision to 10 meters.

The RFC provides examples including a network location, a more precise host location, and a runway at Boston Logan Airport. These examples show how both coarse locations (good for a city block or network) and fine locations (specific buildings or airports) can be encoded.
sections.eli5: You write the location the way humans read maps: degrees, minutes, seconds, then North or South. The computer translates this into the compact number format to store in DNS.

sections.title: Application Use and Search Algorithms
sections.content:
Applications can search for location information in several ways. When looking up a name, the application first checks if that name has a LOC record. If not, it can check the IP addresses associated with that name and look for network or subnet LOC records. When starting with an IP address (as in a visual traceroute), the application reverses the address in the IN-ADDR.ARPA namespace and queries for LOC records at that address and progressively less specific network levels.

This hierarchical search allows administrators to specify locations at the network level without needing separate records for each host. A computer lab with 24 machines on the same subnet would need only one LOC record for the subnet, unless individual machines had been located more precisely elsewhere.
sections.eli5: When you want to know where something is, you ask 'Where is this computer?' and if that doesn't have an answer, you ask 'Where is this network?', working your way up to broader areas until you find one.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The RFC's authors recognized that precise location information poses a security risk. High-precision LOC records could be used to plan physical attacks on specific infrastructure or machines. Publishing exact building coordinates could aid burglary or other crimes. The authors humorously declined to name this record type 'ICBM' to avoid the appearance of encouraging malicious use.

Administrators must consider whether to publish LOC records at all, and if so, whether to use coarse precision values that are less useful for security threats while still supporting applications like network maps.
sections.eli5: If bad people know exactly where your computer is, they could do something mean to it. So you have to decide if you want to tell people where your computer really is.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Must be zero; required for implementations to check.

fields.name: Size
fields.desc: Diameter of sphere in centimeters; encoded as base*10^exponent.

fields.name: Horiz Precision
fields.desc: Horizontal accuracy in centimeters using same encoding as Size.

fields.name: Vert Precision
fields.desc: Vertical accuracy in centimeters using same encoding as Size.

fields.name: Latitude
fields.desc: Latitude in thousandths of seconds of arc; 2^31 is equator.

fields.name: Longitude
fields.desc: Longitude in thousandths of seconds of arc; 2^31 is prime meridian.

fields.name: Altitude
fields.desc: Altitude in centimeters from 100,000m below WGS 84 ellipsoid.
